processing: Anhua raw dark tea is steamed and packed into a bamboo, leaf and smartweed wrapping, then twisted, stomped, rolled and hammered into a tight column. It then dries slowly in the open air.
harvest_season: One maker's lot is listed as spring tea, but it is not generally sold by picking date. As with other Anhua dark teas, the year of pressing is what counts.
appearance_dry: A tight cylinder bound in woven bamboo, with dark, densely compressed tea inside.
appearance_liquor: Orange-yellow to orange-red and clear, deepening with age.
appearance_wet: Dark brown leaf fragments, as with other Anhua dark teas.
taste_profile: Described like its bigger relative, Qian Liang: pine-tinged, thick and mellow, gaining sweetness as it ages.

brewing.notes: Remove the bamboo and cut small pieces; a saw helps. Rinse once, use boiling water, and let chips air for a few days before brewing.

vintage_note: Sold whole by pressing year, often as an aged column, with samples cut from it by some shops. Lots from about ten years ago are easy to find from Western and Chinese sellers. Keep it dry and aired, in its bamboo, and it goes on changing.
description:
Bai Liang Cha is the middle child of the Anhua rolled teas: a bamboo-wrapped column of dark tea, named for a hundred taels, smaller than the famous Qian Liang and larger than Shi Liang. It belongs to the family known as Hua Juan.

The method is the same as for the big columns: steamed raw dark tea is packed into its wrapper and tightened by twisting, stomping, rolling and hammering, then cured in the air. Being smaller, it needs fewer hands, though it is still hard work.

Little has been written about Bai Liang's own taste, so expect what you get from other Anhua rolls: a clean pine note, a thick body and sweetness as it ages. Cut only what you need, and give it boiling water.

The usual weight quoted by one retailer is 3.65 kg, but actual size varies by maker, so check. Look for a named maker and year, and tight, undamaged bamboo. A musty smell is a warning sign.
history:
Little is documented about Bai Liang's own beginnings. One English account says Shanxi merchants of the Sanhe firm developed Qian Liang from Bai Liang in the Tongzhi years, which would make Bai Liang the older tea. A Hunan press account places the start of Qian Liang earlier, in the Jiaqing to Daoguang years, so the order and dates are not settled.

Today it is sold under the wider Anhua Qian Liang family name, along with the ten-tael and thousand-tael sizes.
